annotations.text:
Same turn, same sign, three visual languages — so this is a like-for-like comparison rather than a rigged one.

The item is 出口 (chūkǒu, "way out"). Middle bet shown in all three: +5 / −3.

A · CONTINUITY

Today's dohhh skin, new anatomy. Character at display size inside the existing HeroUI card.

For: ships fastest, one visual system to maintain, a dohhh player is instantly at home.

Against: the character is rendered as app chrome — white-on-violet, rounded, glowing. Nothing in China looks like this, so recognition may not transfer to a station wall.

B · SIGNAGE-LED  ← my recommendation

The card is a sign plate: light field, black hanzi, a domain colour bar. The dark app chrome frames it rather than restyling it.

For: the visual language does pedagogical work. You practise on something that looks like the thing. The domain bar (metro blue / menu red / market yellow / street green) teaches category at a glance.

Against: a light plate in a dark app is a harder composition to keep elegant across every card type, and photo-based sign cards will fight it.

C · EDITORIAL

Near-black, serif, one hairline rule, 132px character and a great deal of air.

For: the most beautiful of the three, and the best for a long solo session — nothing competes with the glyph.

Against: it reads as a study tool, not a game. Weakest at the thing dohhh is actually for — five people round a table with the turn moving fast.

CLICKABLE — tap through the whole turn.

Bet → sign → answer → reveal. "Restart" resets it.

The idea worth arguing about: the bet is how much SCAFFOLDING you give up, not an abstract difficulty label.

  +1 / −1   pinyin shown, answers in English
  +5 / −3   no pinyin
  +15 / −10  no pinyin, and the four answers are signs too

That maps dohhh's existing pre-commitment bet onto something pedagogically real (desirable difficulty + self-calibration) instead of onto "how obscure is this trivia".

Pick "Cold read" to see the four-hanzi variant — it is a different game.

Two tweak chips above the frame: the domain plate colour, and whether tone colour appears at all. Tone colour sits on the PINYIN, never on the character — a learner who recognises a coloured glyph has not learned to read a sign.

Still open, pending the research: whether to gloss in Dutch or English (shown here as both), and whether tone colour helps or becomes a crutch.
